title: Fields and properties (state and accessors)
hook: Fields store data inside an object. Properties are the public door to that data — they look like fields but can validate, compute, or restrict when values change.

blocks.text: A **field** is raw storage inside a type — like a drawer in a cabinet. A **property** is a named accessor with `get` (read) and optionally `set` (write) or `init` (write only during construction). Properties let you change how data is stored later without breaking callers. In C# 14, the `field` keyword inside an accessor refers to a compiler-created backing field so you do not have to name `_payload` yourself.

entries.plainDefinition: A variable declared directly inside a type. Fields hold the actual stored data.
A member that exposes data through get/set/init accessors. Callers use it like a field, but you control access.
entries.example: `public string Name { get; set; }` is an auto-property.

entries.plainDefinition: A setter that only works during object construction — in a constructor or object initializer.
entries.example: `public string Key { get; init; }` can be set in `new Entry { Key = "x" }` but not later.

entries.plainDefinition: A contextual keyword inside a property accessor that refers to the compiler-synthesized backing field.

blocks.text: Public fields freeze your API: once callers read `customer.Name` as a field, you cannot add validation, lazy loading, or change-notification without breaking them. Properties are the versionable surface. The CLR enforces `private` fields — this is not a comment or a convention like TypeScript `private`.

blocks.title: Keep fields private
blocks.body: Expose data through properties. Use `const` for compile-time constants and `static readonly` for one-time runtime initialization. Instance fields plus a constructor are how a cache entry or auth ticket holds its data.

sections.heading: How get, set, and init work

items.title: `get` reads the value
items.body: Called when code reads the property. You can compute a value on the fly or return a stored field.

items.title: `set` mutates after construction
items.body: Called when code assigns to the property after the object exists. Fine for a retry counter; wrong for a token you want frozen after creation.

items.title: `init` restricts to construction
items.body: Legal only in a constructor body or object initializer. After construction, assignment is a compile error.

items.title: Auto-properties
items.body: `{ get; set; }` or `{ get; init; }` still have a hidden backing field. Expression-bodied accessors (`=>`) are shorthand for the same thing.

diagram.title: Property accessor flow
diagram.source:
flowchart TD
  R[Caller reads property] --> G[get accessor]
  G --> F[Backing field or computed value]
  W[Caller writes property] --> S{Accessor type?}
  S -->|set| M[Mutate backing field]
  S -->|init| C{During construction?}
  C -->|yes| M
  C -->|no| E[Compile error]

blocks.title: Accessors in C# vs JS/TS
rows: JS `get name()` / `set name(v)` on objects or classes
No equivalent — use constructor assignment only by convention
TS `constructor(public name: string)` creates a field automatically
TS `private` is erased; JS `#field` is runtime but not metadata

blocks.title: Public mutable fields on DTOs
blocks.body: A public field cannot gain validation later without breaking every caller. Start with private fields and public properties, even on simple data-transfer objects.

blocks.title: `init` is not thread-safe immutability
blocks.body: `{ get; init; }` only restricts assignment to construction time. It does not add synchronization. Sharing a mutable class across threads still needs proper concurrency design (module 15).

interviewTakeaways: Properties are the versionable API; fields are implementation details kept private.
`init` restricts assignment to construction — it is not permanent immutability for the whole object lifetime.
C# 14 `field` removes most manual backing fields; watch for identifier collisions with existing members named `field`.
commonPitfalls: Public mutable fields on DTOs that later need validation.
Assuming `{ get; init; }` makes a class safe to share across threads.

jsTsCorrelations.note: JavaScript getters and setters are similar in spirit but remain a prototype feature without CLR accessibility. There is no `init` accessor.
TypeScript `constructor(public name: string)` creates a field. C# primary constructors plus explicit properties make backing storage and `init` versus `set` visible in the type definition.
